title: Tragedy and Aristotle's Poetics: hamartia, catharsis and the fall of a great person
examples: Why is Oedipus Rex the perfect tragedy?

explain.say: Around 335 BCE, the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote a short book, the Poetics, that still shapes how we talk about tragedy. He called tragedy the imitation of a serious action that arouses pity and fear. The graph shows a shape the German critic Gustav Freytag drew in 1863: rising tension, a climax, a reversal, a fall.

explain.say: Aristotle's favourite example was Sophocles' Oedipus the King. Follow the panels: a plague grips Thebes, and King Oedipus vows to find the murderer of the old king. Clue by clue, he discovers he is the killer, and the old king was his father. A gentle note: the play ends in self-blinding. Why is it worse that his own search undoes him?

explain.say: Sort Aristotle's key words. Hamartia, often called a tragic flaw, is better understood as an error of judgement. Peripeteia is the reversal, when fortune turns. Anagnorisis is the recognition, from ignorance to knowledge. And catharsis is what happens to us: pity and fear released, or perhaps clarified. In Oedipus, which two happen at once?

Not everyone obeys Aristotle. He thought plot mattered most and the hero should be of high standing. Later critics turned his ideas into strict unities of action, time and place, though only unity of action is truly his. In 1949 Arthur Miller argued an ordinary man can be tragic, like Willy Loman in Death of a Salesman. Who convinces you?

explain.say: So tragedy is a shape: a great person, an error, a turn, a recognition, a fall, and in the audience, a release of feeling. Look for it in Hamlet, King Lear, or even a film about a fallen sports star. Superb. Challenge: find the hamartia and the moment of recognition in a tragedy you know.

faq.a: Aristotle's word for what tragedy does to the audience's pity and fear. It may mean purging, cleansing or clarifying those feelings; scholars still debate which, but all agree we leave changed.

An error or mistake of judgement that leads the hero to disaster. It is often translated as tragic flaw, but Aristotle meant a mistake, such as Oedipus not knowing who his parents were, more than a moral vice.

faq.q: Why is Oedipus Rex the perfect tragedy?
faq.a: Aristotle admired it because its recognition and reversal happen at the same moment: the messenger who comes to cheer Oedipus reveals his true identity. The plot is tightly unified and arouses intense pity and fear.
The moment of recognition, when a character moves from ignorance to knowledge, often of who someone really is. Oedipus's discovery of his parentage is the classic example.

Rules of action, time and place, demanding one plot, about one day, one location. Aristotle stressed unity of action and noted plays usually span about a day; unity of place was added by Renaissance critics such as Castelvetro.

facts: Aristotle wrote the Poetics around 335 BCE.
Aristotle names six parts of tragedy: plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle, and ranks plot first.
Gustav Freytag described his five-part dramatic structure, often drawn as a pyramid, in 1863.
